q: In which year was John Galsworthy awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature?
e: John Galsworthy (1867–1933) won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1932 "for his distinguished art of narration which takes its highest form in The Forsyte Saga." He was too ill to attend the ceremony in Stockholm and donated the entire prize money to PEN International. Exam trap: he received the Order of Merit in 1929, not the Nobel Prize.

q: Under what pseudonym did John Galsworthy publish his earliest four works, including 'From the Four Winds' (1897) and 'Jocelyn' (1898)?
e: Galsworthy used the pen name "John Sinjohn" (derived from "son of John", as his father was also named John Galsworthy) for From the Four Winds (1897), Jocelyn (1898), Villa Rubein (1900), and A Man of Devon (1901). He first published under his own name with The Island Pharisees (1904).

q: Which international association of writers elected John Galsworthy as its very first President in 1921?
e: Founded in London in 1921 by Catherine Amy Dawson Scott, the PEN Club (Poets, Essayists, Novelists) elected John Galsworthy as its first President—a role he held until his death in 1933. He later endowed the organization with his 1932 Nobel Prize money.

q: Which novel is the opening book of John Galsworthy's celebrated trilogy 'The Forsyte Saga'?
e: The Man of Property (1906) is the first novel of The Forsyte Saga (1922), followed by In Chancery (1920) and To Let (1921), linked by two interludes: Indian Summer of a Forsyte (1918) and Awakening (1920). The White Monkey opens the second trilogy, A Modern Comedy.

q: Which was John Galsworthy's very first play, staged at the Royal Court Theatre in 1906?
e: The Silver Box (1906) launched Galsworthy's career as a dramatist under Granville-Barker's management at the Royal Court Theatre. It exposes the class bias of the English legal system by contrasting the wealthy Jack Barthwick with the unemployed charwoman's husband, Jones.

q: Which 1910 play by John Galsworthy led directly to prison reforms regarding solitary confinement initiated by Home Secretary Winston Churchill?
e: Justice (1910), depicting the tragic downfall of clerk William Falder through harsh solitary confinement, deeply moved then-Home Secretary Winston Churchill, who subsequently curtailed solitary confinement in British prisons. Exam trap: Justice is a tragedy in four acts, not a comedy.

q: Who is the central figure dubbed "the Man of Property" in 'The Forsyte Saga', whose possessive marriage to Irene drives the narrative?
e: Soames Forsyte, a wealthy Victorian solicitor, epitomizes the acquisitive "sense of property," viewing his beautiful wife Irene Heron as another prized possession. Architect Philip Bosinney falls in love with Irene and is engaged to June Forsyte.

q: What is the central social conflict dramatized in John Galsworthy's 1909 play 'Strife'?
o: Industrial warfare between Capital and Labour
e: Strife (1909) portrays an uncompromising strike at the Trenartha Tin Plate Works, pitting obstinate company chairman John Anthony (Capital) against fanatical union leader David Roberts (Labour). Both extremists are broken, and the strike settles on the exact compromise terms available before it began.

q: Which prestigious British royal honour did John Galsworthy accept in 1929 after having famously declined a knighthood in 1918?
e: Galsworthy declined a knighthood offered by Prime Minister David Lloyd George in 1918 on the principle that "literature is its own reward," but he accepted the prestigious Order of Merit (OM) in 1929.

q: Who is the tragic protagonist of John Galsworthy's play 'Justice' (1910), a junior law clerk who alters a cheque to rescue the woman he loves?
e: William Falder, a weak-willed 23-year-old junior clerk at James and Walter How's law firm, alters a cheque from £9 to £90 to help Ruth Honeywell escape her abusive husband. Robert Cokeson is the sympathetic managing clerk, while Ronald Dancy is the protagonist of Loyalties.

q: Which trilogy by John Galsworthy forms the direct sequel to 'The Forsyte Saga', chronicling the post-World War I generation of Fleur and Michael Mont?
e: A Modern Comedy (published as a single volume in 1929) comprises The White Monkey (1924), The Silver Spoon (1926), and Swan Song (1928), plus two interludes (A Silent Wooing and Passers By). End of the Chapter (1934) is the third trilogy focusing on the Cherrell family.

q: In which 1922 play does John Galsworthy examine anti-Semitism, class loyalty, and professional ethics around the theft of £1,000 at a country house?
e: Loyalties (1922), Galsworthy's greatest commercial theatrical hit, centres on wealthy Jewish guest Ferdinand De Levis accusing war hero Captain Ronald Dancy of stealing £1,000 at Charles Winsor's country house. Every character acts out of conflicting group, club, class, or marital loyalties.

q: Where was John Galsworthy born on 14 August 1867?
e: John Galsworthy was born at Kingston Hill (Kingston upon Thames), Surrey, into a wealthy upper-middle-class legal family—the very social milieu he later satirized in The Forsyte Saga. He died at Grove Lodge, Hampstead, London on 31 January 1933.

q: Which 1920 play by John Galsworthy dramatizes a bitter feud between the old landed aristocracy (the Hillcrists) and a ruthless nouveau-riche industrialist (Mr. Hornblower)?
e: The Skin Game (1920) shows how "gentlemanly" Squire Hillcrist and his wife stoop to blackmailing Hornblower's daughter-in-law Chloe to preserve their estate, asking at the end: "What's gentility worth if it can't stand fire?" Alfred Hitchcock adapted it into a film in 1931.

q: Which celebrated Polish-born British novelist became John Galsworthy's lifelong friend and literary mentor after they met aboard the sailing ship 'Torrens' in 1893?
e: While voyaging from Australia to South Africa aboard the clipper Torrens in 1893, Galsworthy befriended the first mate, Joseph Conrad (then writing Almayer's Folly). Conrad read Galsworthy's early manuscripts and encouraged him to pursue serious fiction.

q: Which two short interludes link the three full-length novels of 'The Forsyte Saga'?
o: A Silent Wooing and Passers By
Salvation of a Forsyte and The Juryman
Indian Summer of a Forsyte and Awakening
e: Indian Summer of a Forsyte (1918, depicting Old Jolyon's tender final days with Irene) links The Man of Property (1906) and In Chancery (1920); Awakening (1920, focusing on young Jon Forsyte) links In Chancery and To Let (1921). A Silent Wooing and Passers By belong to A Modern Comedy.

q: In 'The Silver Box' (1906), what two items are stolen in parallel episodes that expose the double standard of English justice?
o: A gold watch and a cheque book
A pocketbook of £1,000 notes and a hunting rifle
A diamond brooch and a silver candlestick
A lady's reticule (purse) and a silver cigarette box
e: Drunk rich boy Jack Barthwick steals a woman's crimson silk purse (reticule) and escapes prosecution through his MP father's money and influence, whereas unemployed Jones drunkenly steals the Barthwicks' silver cigarette box and receives one month's hard labour.

q: In 'Strife' (1909), whose tragic death from starvation and cold during the harsh winter strike deepens David Roberts's bitterness yet fails to soften John Anthony?
e: Annie Roberts, David Roberts's frail wife, dies of cold and malnutrition caused by the prolonged strike at Trenartha Tin Plate Works. Enid Underwood is John Anthony's compassionate daughter (married to manager Francis Underwood), and Ruth Honeywell belongs to Justice.

q: Who is the defence counsel in 'Justice' (1910) who delivers the famous courtroom speech describing justice as a "machine that, when someone has once given it the starting push, rolls on of itself"?
e: Defence counsel Hector Frome pleads passionately for mercy for William Falder, depicting the law as a blind "chariot" / "machine" that crushes weak individuals like Falder, while Crown prosecutor Harold Cleaver argues strictly for deterrence.

q: How does William Falder meet his death at the close of Act IV of 'Justice' (1910)?
o: He is hanged at Pentonville Prison
He dies of pneumonia in solitary confinement
He throws himself down a stone staircase to escape rearrest for failing to report on ticket-of-leave
He shoots himself in his bedroom with a revolver
e: Released on ticket-of-leave, Falder is hounded from jobs, fails to report to the police, and forges a reference; when Detective-Sergeant Wister arrives to rearrest him at the Hows' office, Falder breaks away and leaps down the stairs, breaking his neck. Cokeson closes the play: "No one'll touch him now! Never again! He's safe with gentle Jesus!"

q: In 'The Man of Property' (1906), what architectural project does Soames Forsyte commission Philip Bosinney to design, which becomes the focal point of Soames's legal vendetta?
o: A country house at Robin Hill
e: Soames commissions Bosinney to build a country house at Robin Hill to isolate Irene from London society; when Bosinney exceeds the budget and falls in love with Irene, Soames sues him into financial ruin. Bosinney dies after being struck by a bus in thick London fog.

q: In 'Loyalties' (1922), how is Captain Ronald Dancy's guilt conclusively proved, leading to his suicide?
o: A servant confesses to helping him climb the balcony
Ferdinand De Levis withdraws his accusation in exchange for a signed confession
His wife Mabel finds the missing cash hidden in his coat
The serial numbers of the stolen £1,000 notes are traced through grocer Gilman and Italian wine-merchant Ricardos, whose daughter Dancy had paid off
e: Grocer Gilman brings a £50 note to solicitor Jacob Twisden (who is defending Dancy against De Levis's slander counter-action); the note is traced to Ricardos, who confirms Dancy paid him £1,000 hush-money for his daughter's affair. Faced with arrest, Dancy shoots himself leaving a note: "A pistol keeps faith."

q: Which 1904 novel was the FIRST book published under John Galsworthy's real name and launched his sustained critique of upper-middle-class English complacency?
e: The Island Pharisees (1904), featuring protagonist Richard Shelton and the cynical Belgian vagabond Louis Ferrand, was Galsworthy's first work under his own name. He later reused the vagabond figure Ferrand in his 1912 play The Pigeon.

q: Who is the warm-hearted, impractical artist in Galsworthy's 'The Pigeon' (1912) who compulsively gives shelter and money to social outcasts ("wild birds"), satirizing both sentimental charity and rigid institutional reform?
e: Christopher Wellwyn is the "pigeon" plucked by three misfits—French vagabond Ferrand, alcoholic cabman Timson, and flower-seller Guinevere Megan—while three dogmatic reformers (a Canon, a Professor, and a Justice of the Peace) fail to cure them.

q: What is the central theme of John Galsworthy's 1912 play 'The Eldest Son'?
o: Class hypocrisy in aristocratic sexual morality and marriage
e: In The Eldest Son (written 1909, staged 1912), Sir William Cheshire insists that under-keeper Dunning must marry the village girl he made pregnant, yet violently forbids his own eldest son Bill from marrying Freda Studdenham (Lady Cheshire's maid) when she is expecting Bill's child.

q: In 'Swan Song' (1928), the concluding novel of 'A Modern Comedy', how does Soames Forsyte die?
o: Of a heart attack during a courtroom trial
Struck by an omnibus in London fog
Drowning in the River Thames while boating
Saving his daughter Fleur from a falling picture frame during a fire in his picture gallery at Mapledurham
e: Soames Forsyte dies heroically in Swan Song (1928) after rescuing his beloved daughter Fleur from a heavy falling painting during a fire in his picture gallery—a poignant redemption for "the Man of Property." (It was Philip Bosinney who died in London fog in The Man of Property.)

q: Which posthumous 1934 trilogy forms the third and final part of Galsworthy's Forsyte Chronicles, centring on Dinny Cherrell?
e: End of the Chapter (published posthumously in 1934) brings together Maid in Waiting (1931), Flowering Wilderness (1932), and Over the River (1933), following Dinny Cherrell, cousin to Michael Mont. Caravan (1925) is Galsworthy's collected short stories.

q: In Galsworthy's 1926 episodic play 'Escape', who is the gentleman convict who escapes from Dartmoor Prison after accidentally killing a plainclothes policeman in Hyde Park?
e: Captain Matt Denant escapes from Dartmoor in a fog and encounters a cross-section of English society across nine episodes before voluntarily surrendering in a country church rather than forcing a parson to tell a lie.

q: Which 1914 play by John Galsworthy depicts an idealistic MP, Stephen More, who stands alone against jingoistic war fever and is killed by an angry patriotic crowd?
e: The Mob (1914) dramatizes the tragedy of Under-Secretary of State Stephen More, who opposes an unjust imperial war against a small nation, loses his seat, wife, and life to mob fury, yet is posthumously vindicated by a statue.

q: In his celebrated 1909 essay 'Some Platitudes Concerning Drama', what does John Galsworthy call the unifying moral idea that must organically shape every serious play?
e: In Some Platitudes Concerning Drama (1909, collected in The Inn of Tranquillity, 1912), Galsworthy asserts that "Every grouping of life and character has its inherent moral; and the business of the dramatist is so to pose the group as to bring that moral poignantly to the light of day"—creating what he calls "The Spire of Meaning."

q: Whom did John Galsworthy marry in 1905 after a ten-year secret relationship while she was unhappily married to his cousin Arthur Galsworthy, inspiring the character of Irene in 'The Forsyte Saga'?
e: Ada Nemesis Pearson Cooper was married to Galsworthy's cousin Arthur; her unhappy marriage and divorce (1905) directly inspired Irene's trapped marriage to Soames in The Man of Property. Galsworthy dedicated The Forsyte Saga to Ada.

q: In 'To Let' (1921), why does the passionate young love between Fleur Forsyte (Soames's daughter) and Jon Forsyte (Young Jolyon and Irene's son) end in separation?
o: Jon is killed in World War I
Fleur refuses to give up her family inheritance
Jon learns the bitter truth of how Soames once mistreated his mother Irene and refuses to wound her by marrying Soames's daughter
Soames legally forbids Fleur from marrying a painter's son
e: Upon reading his late father Young Jolyon's letter revealing Soames's marital cruelty to Irene, Jon chooses loyalty to his mother over Fleur; Fleur marries Michael Mont on the rebound, and Robin Hill is left "To Let."

q: Which Galsworthy play (1915) focuses on curate Michael Strangway, whose gentle Christian forgiveness toward his unfaithful wife shocks his intolerant rural parish?
e: A Bit o' Love (1915) portrays Michael Strangway, a saintly young curate who frees his wife Beatrice to live with her lover and even lets a caged skylark go, only to be condemned as weak by his parishioners until a child restores his will to live.

q: Which literary movement and dramatic genre is John Galsworthy most closely associated with in early twentieth-century British theatre?
e: Following Ibsen and alongside Shaw and Granville-Barker, Galsworthy mastered the Naturalistic Social Problem Play, using restrained everyday dialogue, balanced opposing viewpoints, and sharp structural irony to expose institutional injustice.

q: Which novel by John Galsworthy (1907) satirizes the conservative English squirearchy through the Pendyce family of Worsted Skeynes?
e: The Country House (1907) portrays Horace Pendyce and the landed gentry's rigid "Pendycitis." Galsworthy's other social-class novels include Fraternity (1909, middle-class intellectuals vs slums), The Patrician (1911, aristocracy), and The Freelands (1915, agricultural labourers).

q: Which famous modernist novelist attacked John Galsworthy (along with H. G. Wells and Arnold Bennett) as a "materialist" obsessed with external social details rather than inner consciousness in the 1924 essay 'Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown'?
e: In Modern Fiction (1919) and Mr. Bennett and Mrs. Brown (1924), Virginia Woolf grouped Galsworthy, Wells, and Bennett as Edwardian "materialists" who focused on social fabric and property rather than the inner "luminous halo" of consciousness.

q: Which twentieth-century novelist launched a scathing 1928 essay titled 'John Galsworthy', accusing Galsworthy's Forsytes of lacking true vital passion and calling them "social beings" reduced to money-consciousness?
e: D. H. Lawrence's famous 1928 critique 'John Galsworthy' (published in Scrutinies, ed. Edgell Rickword) argued that Galsworthy's satire remained trapped inside the very bourgeois values he mocked, contrasting "human beings" with "social beings."

q:
Match List-I (Galsworthy Play) with List-II (Key Character) and select the correct code:
1. The Silver Box — (a) Ferdinand De Levis
2. Strife — (b) William Falder
3. Justice — (c) David Roberts
4. Loyalties — (d) John Barthwick, MP
e: The Silver Box features Liberal MP John Barthwick (1-d); Strife features strike leader David Roberts (2-c); Justice features clerk William Falder (3-b); Loyalties features Ferdinand De Levis (4-a).

q: In 'Justice' (1910), which silent, wordless scene in Act III Scene 3 became one of the most famous theatrical moments of the twentieth century?
o: Ruth Honeywell sitting silently outside the Old Bailey
William Falder pacing his cramped solitary cell in rising panic and beating frantically on the iron door
Robert Cokeson burning the forged cheque in the law office
The Judge pronouncing sentence while the courtroom sits in darkness
e: Act III Scene 3 of Justice contains zero spoken dialogue—only detailed stage directions showing William Falder pacing his tiny cell, listening to distant hammering, and finally hurling himself against the cell door in psychological breakdown. This scene directly spurred Winston Churchill's prison reforms.

q: What are the memorable closing lines of 'Strife' (1909), spoken by Secretary Harness to Tench after both John Anthony and David Roberts have been destroyed?
o: "No one'll touch him now! Never again!"
"A woman dead; and the two best men both broken! ... That's where the fun comes in!"
"Keep faith! We've all done that. It's not enough."
"What's gentility worth if it can't stand fire?"
e: In Strife, trade-union official Simon Harness remarks bitterly to Tench that the final settlement terms are identical to those drafted before the strike: "A woman dead; and the two best men both broken! ... That's where the fun comes in!" (Option A is Justice; C is Loyalties; D is The Skin Game.)

q: Which closing line of 'Loyalties' (1922), spoken by Margaret Orme beside Ronald Dancy's dead body, encapsulates the play's central irony?
o: "We've all been loyal. Keep faith! We've all done that. It's not enough."
"The law is what it is—a majestic edifice, sheltering all of us."
"It is not the strongest who survive, but the gentlest."
"There is nothing either good or bad, but loyalty makes it so."
e: Margaret Orme's final words—"Keep faith! We've all done that. It's not enough."—crystallize Galsworthy's thesis that narrow tribal, club, or class loyalties without higher moral truth breed tragedy. (Option B is the Judge's ironic line in Justice.)

q: In his 1922 Preface to 'The Forsyte Saga', how does John Galsworthy famously summarize the overarching theme of the entire Saga?
o: "The triumph of Victorian capitalism over feudal aristocracy"
"The impingement of Beauty, and the claims of Freedom, on a possessive world"
"The decline of the British Empire after the Boer War"
"The tragedy of artistic genius crushed by industrial labour"
e: In his 1922 Preface, Galsworthy states that the Saga depicts "the impingement of Beauty, and the claims of Freedom, on a possessive world," noting that Irene represents "a concretion of disturbing Beauty impinging on a possessive world" (the Forsyte clan).

q: What was the title of John Galsworthy's VERY FIRST published book (1897), a collection of four short stories issued at his own expense under the pseudonym John Sinjohn?
e: From the Four Winds (1897) was Galsworthy's debut publication (short stories), later suppressed by him as immature. His first novel was Jocelyn (1898), followed by Villa Rubein (1900) and A Man of Devon (1901, which introduced the Forsytes in the story "The Salvation of a Forsyte").

q: In which 1901 story (published in 'A Man of Devon' under the name John Sinjohn) did the Forsyte family make their VERY FIRST appearance in print?
e: "The Salvation of a Forsyte" (in A Man of Devon, 1901) introduced Swithin Forsyte and the Forsyte clan five years before The Man of Property (1906). Exam trap: most candidates mistakenly pick The Man of Property or Indian Summer of a Forsyte.

q: How does John Galsworthy's dramatic technique fundamentally differ from that of his contemporary George Bernard Shaw?
o: Galsworthy uses verse dialogue, whereas Shaw uses prose
Galsworthy aims for detached, impartial presentation of both sides without a mouthpiece character, whereas Shaw uses witty intellectual debate and a dominant raisonneur/mouthpiece
Galsworthy writes historical romances, whereas Shaw writes kitchen-sink realism
Galsworthy avoids stage directions completely, whereas Shaw writes lengthy prefaces
e: Unlike Shaw's sparkling paradoxical debates and didactic spokespersons, Galsworthy strives for scrupulous impartiality ("holding the scales even"), allowing tragic irony to emerge naturally from realistic characters trapped in flawed institutions.

q: Which 1924 play by John Galsworthy features the indomitable, epicurean eighty-year-old shipowner Sylvanus Heythorp (adapted from his own short story 'A Stoic')?
e: Old English (1924), adapted from Galsworthy's 1918 story "A Stoic," centres on crusty, defiant octogenarian Sylvanus Heythorp ("Old English"), who enjoys one last lavish dinner and dies on his own terms rather than face financial disgrace.

q: In 'A Modern Comedy', which libel lawsuit between Fleur Mont and Marjorie Ferrar dominates the plot of 'The Silver Spoon' (1926)?
o: A dispute over copyright of a painting at Robin Hill
A slander/libel action after Soames calls Marjorie Ferrar a "traitress" and Fleur labels her a "snob" with "no morals"
A breach-of-promise suit filed by Jon Forsyte
A defamation suit brought by Michael Mont in the House of Commons
e: In The Silver Spoon (1926), social rivalry between Fleur Mont and modernist bohemian Marjorie Ferrar erupts into a sensational London libel trial that exposes the hollowness of 1920s "Foggartism" and post-war society.

q: Which was John Galsworthy's FINAL full-length play, produced in 1929, depicting guests trapped in different rooms of a burning Paris hotel?
e: The Roof (1929) was Galsworthy's last staged play, using simultaneous scenes in a burning Paris hotel to reveal how ordinary people behave under sudden mortal crisis. Exiled was staged earlier in 1929; Escape in 1926; The Show in 1925.

q: Which celebrated 1912 short story by John Galsworthy poignantly portrays the Gessler brothers, German bootmakers in London driven to starvation by mass-produced factory boots?
e: "Quality" (published in The Inn of Tranquillity, 1912) is one of Galsworthy's most anthologized short stories, contrasting artisanal integrity (Mr. Gessler) with soulless commercial advertising and industrial mass production.

q:
Consider the following two statements about John Galsworthy's literary career:
Statement I: Galsworthy was called to the Bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1890, and his legal training deeply shaped the courtroom realism of 'The Silver Box', 'Justice', and 'Loyalties'.
Statement II: In 'The Forsyte Saga', Old Jolyon dies peacefully under an oak tree at Robin Hill in 'Indian Summer of a Forsyte' after leaving a legacy to Irene.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
o: Both Statement I and Statement II
Neither Statement I nor Statement II
e: Both statements are completely accurate: Galsworthy studied law at New College, Oxford and was called to the Bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1890 (though he barely practised), and Old Jolyon's serene death beneath the oak at Robin Hill closes the interlude Indian Summer of a Forsyte (1918).
